items.title: 8.16.1 Synthesis of ammonia by Haber's process

source_refs.note: Topic 8.16.1, printed pages 183-184, with Table 8.1 and Fig 8.4.

blocks.text: It is one of the basic needs of industry to have maximum yield of the product. We can apply the concept of equilibrium in order to have the maximum yield from the industrial synthesis of ammonia.
Ammonia synthesis from nitrogen and hydrogen is a reversible process.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: −46.11 kJ is the enthalpy change per mole of NH₃ formed. For the equation as written, which forms 2 mol NH₃, ΔH = 2 × (−46.11) = −92.2 kJ (the table of Quick Check 8.6 gives −92 kJ mol⁻¹). The sign and the conclusions are unchanged.
The maximum yield of ammonia can be achieved by the following ways:

items: Decrease the concentration of ammonia by removing it from the reaction vessel from time to time. Equilibrium will shift to the forward direction in accordance with Le-Chatelier’s principle.

Since, four moles of reactants combine to give two moles of products, reaction happens with the decreasing volume. High pressure will shift the equilibrium position to the right to give more and more ammonia.
This is an exothermic reaction. By decreasing temperature, it will shift to the forward direction according to Le-Chatelier’s principle.

blocks.text: When we look at the Table 8.2 given below and the Figure 8.3, then it becomes clear that the effect of pressure and temperature on the yield of ammonia is very prominent. The most complete conversion is 98.3% at 473 K (200 °C) and 1000 atmospheric pressure.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The table and figure meant here are Table 8.1 and Fig 8.4, printed below. Table 8.2 (SO₃ formation) and Figure 8.3 (effect of a catalyst) are about other things.

blocks.caption: Table (8.1): Effect of Temperature on Kc for Ammonia Synthesis.

blocks.alt: Graph of the yield of NH3 (%) from 0 to 100 against temperature from 200 to 700 °C, with five falling curves labelled 1000 atm, 600 atm, 300 atm, 100 atm and 10 atm. At 200 °C the yields are about 98, 95, 90, 81 and 50 %; all fall at higher temperature. A small circle at about 400 °C and 43 %, between the 100 atm and 300 atm curves, has an arrow to the label Industrial conditions.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.4: Percent yield of ammonia vs. Temperature (°C) at five different operating pressures. At very high pressure and low temperature (top left), the yield is high, but the rate of formation is low. Industrial conditions (circle) are between 200 and 300 atm at about 400 °C (original drawing).

blocks.text: At 200 °C, the yield is being favoured but the rate of reaction becomes very slow and the process becomes uneconomical. So, the temperature is raised to a moderate level i.e. 400 °C and a catalyst is used to increase the rate. If we want to achieve the same rate without a catalyst then we require much higher temperature, which lowers the yield.
Optimum conditions to get best yield of ammonia
The most suitable conditions to get maximum yield of ammonia are:

items: Pieces of iron crystals present in a fused mixture of MgO, Al₂O₃ and SiO₂, as catalyst
